provisioning:The Saturday market.name: The Saturday market
provisioning:The Saturday market.teaser: Shop the producers before ten, then eat hot snails from the traiteur's stall standing up
provisioning:The Saturday market.story: Bring a cool bag and a list. Work from the cheese stalls outward: an Époisses and a Cîteaux for the board, a slab of jambon persillé, a pot of Fallot mustard from its own stand, and in late October the girolles and ceps the hill-village growers bring down. When the bags are full, the rotating traiteur's hot snails in garlic butter or a portion of roast chicken is breakfast.
provisioning:The Saturday market.why: Buy the cheese first, while the producers still have the full range on the trestles.
facts: Époisses and Cîteaux cheese, jambon persillé, Fallot mustard, autumn mushrooms; hot snails or roast chicken from the traiteur

provisioning:The Wednesday market.name: The Wednesday market
provisioning:The Wednesday market.teaser: Fifteen or so food stalls under the Halle on a Wednesday morning, and room to talk to each one
provisioning:The Wednesday market.story: Mid-week, the market shrinks to its core: around fifteen traders, food only, gathered on the Place de la Halle where the Saturday crowd fills three squares. That is the point of coming. With no queue, the cheesemaker has time to cut you a taste and the grower time to say what was picked this week. It is the morning to restock the galley between two Saturdays, the list short and the bags light enough to carry back to the car in one trip.

provisioning:Charcuterie Raillard.teaser: Jambon persillé, pâté en croûte and gougères on rue Monge, to carry back for the crew's table

Ask for jambon persillé cut thick and wrapped for the cool bag, a length of pâté en croûte for slicing on board, and a bag of gougères to warm through before the first bottle is opened. If you need a large piece for a guest lunch, ask the day before rather than hoping on the morning.

provisioning:Edmond Fallot.name: Edmond Fallot
provisioning:Edmond Fallot.teaser: Granite millstones still crush the seed at the last family mustard mill in Burgundy, on the faubourg
provisioning:Edmond Fallot.story: The house began in 1840 with Léon Bouley, a miller who made mustard from Burgundian seed. Edmond Fallot bought it in 1928, gave it his name and kept the granite millstones, and his grandson Marc Désarménien runs it today; the family calls it the last independent moutarderie of Burgundy. The stones grind slowly, so the paste stays cool and keeps its heat. The tour ends in a sharp smell of crushed seed and vinegar. Buy the Moutarde de Bourgogne IGP, made from seed grown in Burgundy and Burgundy white wine.
provisioning:Edmond Fallot.why: Take the hour-long tour, then buy the pot marked Moutarde de Bourgogne IGP: Burgundy seed, Burgundy wine.

provisioning:Mulot & Petitjean.name: Mulot & Petitjean
provisioning:Mulot & Petitjean.teaser: The Dijon pain d'épices house, founded in 1796, keeps a shop on Place Carnot
provisioning:Mulot & Petitjean.story: Barnabé Boittier opened a spice-bread shop on rue du Prétoire in Dijon in 1796; under the Mulot & Petitjean name the house celebrated 225 years in 2021. Its Beaune shop on Place Carnot sells the honey-dark loaves by the slice and the nonnettes, small round iced spice cakes with a fruit filling, in boxes that survive a trip in a crew bag. Inside, the shop smells of honey and warm spice. The old guide's pairing still holds: a thin slice under foie gras, or with a strong cheese.

provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.name: Fromagerie Alain Hess
provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.teaser: A Meilleur Ouvrier de France on Place Carnot, and his mustard-seed Délice de Pommard
provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.story: Alain Hess took the Meilleur Ouvrier de France title as a fromager in 1997 and moved his shop onto Place Carnot in 2005. Around 200 cheeses fill the counters, with wine, charcuterie and Italian and Spanish fine food behind. The one to buy is made in-house: the Délice de Pommard, a small triple-crème ball of about 100 g, rolled in mustard seed, named for the village where the first Hess workshop stood. It cuts like butter, then the seeds crack between the teeth.
provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.why: Ask for an Époisses and a Délice de Pommard ready to eat today, and build the cheese board from there.
facts: Délice de Pommard; Époisses, Cîteaux and aged cheeses; jambon persillé; wine

provisioning:Époisses at Berthaut.name: Époisses at Berthaut
provisioning:Époisses at Berthaut.teaser: The family that brought Époisses back from extinction after the war, still making it in the village
provisioning:Époisses at Berthaut.story: By the end of the Second World War the farms of Époisses no longer made the cheese at all. In 1956 Robert Berthaut and his wife started again with milk from their own cows and an aunt's recipe (some sources say around 1960). Their revival carried the cheese to an AOC in 1991 and European protection in 1996. The firm still works in the village, washing each rind in brine and marc de Bourgogne until it turns orange, sticky and loud; it also makes Soumaintrain.
provisioning:Époisses at Berthaut.why: Buy a Berthaut Époisses on the Beaune market or at a fromager rather than drive out: the cheese travels to you.

provisioning:The cheese of Cîteaux.name: The cheese of Cîteaux
provisioning:The cheese of Cîteaux.teaser: At the mother house of the Cistercians, founded 1098, the monks have made one cheese since 1925
provisioning:The cheese of Cîteaux.story: The abbey that sent monks across Europe, and planted the Clos de Vougeot, now lives off a single soft cheese. The community at Cîteaux has made it since 1925: a supple, washed-rind disc in the reblochon family, from raw milk, about 140,000 cheeses a year by a 2021 count. It is sold at the abbey shop by the gate and at a few fromagers. Taste it at room temperature: mild, milky, with a faint cellar smell from the rind.
provisioning:The cheese of Cîteaux.why: Stop at the abbey shop on a Côte de Nuits day; this is a working monastery, so keep voices low.

walks:The ramparts circuit.name: The ramparts circuit
walks:The ramparts circuit.teaser: Two kilometres and more of medieval wall, bastions and moat, best under the plane trees at first light
walks:The ramparts circuit.story: Leave the Place de la Halle early and cut west through rue d'Enfer, where cold air breathes from the cellar vents at ankle height. Climb onto the Rempart des Dames: a double row of plane trees about two hundred years old, its name tied to the Bernardine nuns who lived by the tower. Below, the moat is gardens now. Follow the wall round past the bastions, one of them, Saint-Martin, from the Thirty Years' War; others still hold négociant cellars, Chanson's wine among them. Private stretches break the loop, so step down and pick the wall up again.
walks:The ramparts circuit.why: The Rempart des Dames before the boulangeries open, with nobody else under the trees.
facts: Place de la Halle, by the tourist office
About 2 to 2.5 km round the old town
About an hour; 1-2 hours with detours

walks:The Parc de la Bouzaise loop.name: The Parc de la Bouzaise loop
walks:The Parc de la Bouzaise loop.teaser: Five hectares of English park around the spring that gave Beaune its water, ten minutes from the cellars
walks:The Parc de la Bouzaise loop.story: The town needed water, so its mayor Paul Bouchard bought the land around the source of the Bouzaise from 1886; the park was laid out in the English manner, winding paths around a pond, and listed in 1949. Walk the loop slowly. Ducks and swans work the water, a bronze Béléna by Irénée Duriez stands on the island by the spring's outflow, and the spillway is heard before it is seen. On a weekday morning, after the dog walkers, the bench facing the lake is the quietest seat in Beaune.

walks:Up into the climats.name: Up into the climats
walks:Up into the climats.teaser: From the park gate, two hundred metres of lane and you are walking between premier cru vines
walks:Up into the climats.story: Leave the Parc de la Bouzaise by its western side and take the vineyard lanes uphill. Within about 200 metres the houses stop and the stone walls of the premier crus begin: the Clos des Mouches first, then Les Grèves higher on the slope. The lanes are farm tracks shared with tractors, so step aside and keep off the rows. In late October the leaves have turned yellow and rust, the pickers are gone and the pruners not yet arrived. Turn round near the top: the town's roofs, the plain and the Côte to the south.
walks:Up into the climats.why: The view back over Beaune from the top of the slope, with the autumn vines below you.

walks:Beaune to Meursault by the vines.teaser: Through Pommard and up to Volnay, then down to Meursault, with a train or bus back to Beaune
walks:Beaune to Meursault by the vines.story: Walk out of Beaune south through its own premier crus and into Pommard, past the walls of the Clos des Épeneaux to the village church. Climb to Volnay on the hill, then drop through Monthélie into Meursault, the white-wine village. In late October, the cuveries along the way smell of pressed skins and new wine. Do not walk back: Meursault has its own station on the Dijon-Chalon line.

walks:Corton hill from Pernand-Vergeless.name: Corton hill from Pernand-Vergelesses
walks:Corton hill from Pernand-Vergeless.teaser: Climb from Pernand to the Notre-Dame de Bonne-Espérance lookout, Corton-Charlemagne below your feet
walks:Corton hill from Pernand-Vergeless.story: Pernand-Vergelesses sits in a fold below the wooded crown of the Corton hill, which carries a red grand cru, Corton, and a white one. From the village the paths climb through that white, Corton-Charlemagne, about 72 hectares in all, 17 of them in Pernand, to the statue of Notre-Dame de Bonne-Espérance at about 490 metres, with an orientation table, Beaune and the Saône plain spread out below. The story goes that Charlemagne owned vines here and had white grapes planted so that red wine would not stain his beard: a legend, nothing more. In October the slope goes gold.
walks:Corton hill from Pernand-Vergeless.why: The orientation table at Notre-Dame de Bonne-Espérance in October, with the whole hill turning gold.

around:The Route des Grands Crus.name: The Route des Grands Crus
around:The Route des Grands Crus.teaser: France's oldest signposted wine road, 60 km from Dijon to Santenay through the grand cru villages
around:The Route des Grands Crus.story: The Côte-d'Or département created it in 1937, in the wake of France's first paid holidays: a 60-kilometre road from Dijon to Santenay, marked by brown signs with a bunch of grapes, through 37 or 38 villages depending on who counts. It runs along the foot of the slope, so the names on the village signs are the names on wine labels: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée, Nuits-Saint-Georges, then Aloxe-Corton, Pommard, Meursault. Since 4 July 2015 the vineyard landscape it crosses, the Climats, has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
around:The Route des Grands Crus.why: Drive it slowly with one dry driver, stopping in the villages rather than at the roadside cellars.
facts: Join it at the edge of Beaune; Dijon is the northern end, Santenay the southern

around:Pommard and Volnay.name: Pommard and Volnay
around:Pommard and Volnay.teaser: A walled château vineyard in Pommard, then the hill village of Volnay just above it
around:Pommard and Volnay.story: Pommard, about 4 km south of Beaune, is a village of cellar doors around a church, with the Château de Pommard at its edge: a house founded in 1726 by one account, a 20-hectare walled clos and a tasting room where the Clos Marey-Monge is poured. The wine is the deep, firm red of the Côte. Volnay sits higher, its houses stepped up the slope, and its reds are lighter, perfumed. Between the two villages the vines change in a few hundred metres; that is the lesson of the Côte in one walk. Rootstock plays in the château's clos in July.
around:Pommard and Volnay.why: Taste a Pommard and a Volnay on the same day and the climat idea stops being abstract.
facts: About 4 km south of Beaune by road or on foot

around:Clos de Vougeot.name: Clos de Vougeot
around:Clos de Vougeot.teaser: The Cistercian wine house in the middle of a walled grand cru, with four giant medieval presses
around:Clos de Vougeot.story: The monks of Cîteaux pieced the clos together from 1109-1115 onward and built the winery in the 12th century; a château was added later. Inside, four huge timber presses stand in the cuverie, beams the size of tree trunks, and the Grand Cellier shows a film on the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin, the brotherhood founded in 1934 that holds its chapitres here; November's is on the hot board. Outside, the clos wall still runs round the vines the monks assembled, and the cellar air is cold and smells of old oak.
around:Clos de Vougeot.why: The presses: the scale of medieval winemaking, in timber, under one roof.
facts: North of Beaune on the Route des Grands Crus, past Nuits-Saint-Georges, by car or with a driver

around:Dijon.name: Dijon
around:Dijon.teaser: The dukes' tombs free to see, an iron market hall, and a new cité of French food by the old hospital
around:Dijon.story: Start in the Palais des Ducs, where the Musée des Beaux-Arts keeps the tombs of Philip the Bold and John the Fearless in the Salle des Gardes: alabaster mourners in hooded robes, each a different grief. The permanent collections are free. Walk to Les Halles, the iron-and-glass market of the 1870s, built to plans inspired by Gustave Eiffel's company, for the cheese and charcuterie stalls. Then cross to the Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin, opened on 6 May 2022 in the old general hospital. Mulot & Petitjean began here.
around:Dijon.why: The hooded alabaster mourners round the ducal tombs, free to see, then lunch near Les Halles.
facts: Direct TER train from Beaune on the Dijon line (check the timetable); about 45 minutes by car
